quote: Capability is defined as the individual's psychological and physical capacity to engage in the activity concerned. It includes having the necessary knowledge and skills. Motivation is defined as all those brain processes that energize and direct behaviour ... Opportunity is defined as all the factors that lie outside the individual that make the behaviour possible or prompt it.
claim: COM-B model: behaviour depends on capability (physical and psychological, including knowledge and skills), opportunity (everything outside the person that makes the behaviour possible or prompts it) and motivation (reflective decisions plus habits and emotional responses). Use it to classify why an athlete is not training as planned before choosing a fix.
population: general framework, not tested specifically in sport coaching
used_for: intake and check-in barrier analysis (what is missing: capability, opportunity or motivation)
caveat: Framework for analysis; it does not itself show that coaching built on it improves adherence.

quote: Education | Increasing knowledge or understanding ... Persuasion | Using communication to induce positive or negative feelings or stimulate action ... Training | Imparting skills ... Environmental restructuring | Changing the physical or social context ... Modelling | Providing an example for people to aspire to or imitate ... Enablement | Increasing means/reducing barriers to increase capability or opportunity
claim: Behaviour Change Wheel intervention functions usable by a coach include education (knowledge), persuasion (feelings or prompting action), training (skills), environmental restructuring (changing physical or social context), modelling (examples to imitate) and enablement (reducing barriers). Match the function to the COM-B deficit, for example training for a skill gap and environmental restructuring for an opportunity gap.
population: general framework
used_for: choosing the type of help after a barrier is identified
caveat: Coercion and restriction are also BCW functions but are not appropriate in voluntary coaching.

quote: This resulted in 93 BCTs clustered into 16 groups.
claim: The Behaviour Change Technique Taxonomy v1 lists 93 distinct techniques in 16 groups (for example goal setting, self-monitoring, action planning, problem solving, prompts/cues, graded tasks); it is a shared vocabulary for describing what a coach actually does.
population: reporting taxonomy, all behaviours
used_for: naming techniques consistently in the knowledge base and coach notes
caveat: A description tool; effectiveness of individual techniques comes from the meta-analyses below.

quote: The technique, "self-monitoring," explained the greatest amount of among-study heterogeneity (13%). Interventions that combined self-monitoring with at least one other technique derived from control theory were significantly more effective than the other interventions (0.42 vs. 0.26).
claim: In physical activity and healthy eating interventions, self-monitoring was the single technique that explained most of the variation in effectiveness; combining self-monitoring with at least one other technique derived from control theory (the self-regulation family) gave larger effects (effect size 0.42 vs 0.26).
population: adults in 122 physical activity and healthy eating intervention evaluations (N = 44,747)
used_for: core check-in loop: log training, compare with the goal, give feedback, review the goal
caveat: Meta-regression is observational across studies; abstract only, so the exact list of control-theory techniques was not read.

quote: Physical activity interventions were effective at changing behavior (d = 0.32, 95% confidence intervals = 0.16-0.48, n = 2,346) and maintaining behavior change after 6 months or more (d = 0.21, 95% confidence intervals = 0.12-0.30, n = 2,190).
claim: In healthy inactive adults, physical activity interventions produced a small effect at the end of the intervention (d = 0.32) and a smaller but still significant effect 6 months or more later (d = 0.21); expect some decay after support ends.
number: d = 0.32 (0.16-0.48) post-intervention; d = 0.21 (0.12-0.30) at 6 months or more
population: healthy inactive adults in RCTs with at least 6 months follow-up (16 pooled studies)
used_for: setting expectations for the sedentary beginner; planning support beyond the first months

quote: At follow-up, effectiveness was associated with using "Action planning," "Instruction on how to perform the behavior," "Prompts/cues," "Behavior practice/rehearsal," "Graded tasks," and "Self-reward."
claim: Maintenance of physical activity in inactive adults was associated with action planning (when, where, what), instruction on how to perform the exercise, prompts and cues, practice/rehearsal, graded tasks (start easy, progress step by step) and self-reward.
population: healthy inactive adults, follow-up 6 months or more
used_for: technique selection for long-term adherence in beginners
caveat: Associations from subgroup analyses of a small number of trials; not proof that each technique works alone.

quote: The 32 long term reports had an overall ES = 0.24 with 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.15 to 0.33 and I2 = 59.4%. The 50 short term reports had an ES = 0.37 with 95% CI: 0.26 to 0.48
claim: In adults with obesity, physical activity and healthy eating interventions had a small effect in the short term (up to 6 months, ES 0.37) and a smaller effect at 12 months or later (ES 0.24).
number: ES 0.37 (0.26-0.48) short term; ES 0.24 (0.15-0.33) long term
population: adults with mean age 40 or more and mean BMI 30 or more, RCTs of at least 12 weeks
used_for: setting realistic expectations; planning for maintenance

quote: The results support the use of goal setting and self-monitoring of behaviour when counselling overweight and obese adults. Several other BCTs as well as the use of a person-centred and autonomy supportive counselling approach seem important in order to maintain behaviour over time.
claim: Use goal setting and self-monitoring of behaviour; for long-term maintenance, add a person-centred, autonomy-supportive counselling style (as in motivational interviewing) and feedback on the outcome of behaviour.
population: adults with obesity (mean BMI 30 or more)
used_for: default technique set for check-ins

quote: using the BCTs goal setting of outcome, feedback on outcome of behaviour, implementing graded tasks, and adding objects to the environment, e.g. using a step counter, significantly predicted the effect at long term.
claim: Long-term effects were predicted by outcome goals, feedback on the outcome of behaviour, graded tasks and adding objects to the environment such as a step counter.
population: adults with obesity (mean BMI 30 or more)
used_for: long-term technique selection; justification for tracker use
caveat: Meta-regression associations, not causal tests.

quote: The results show consistent support for a positive relation between more autonomous forms of motivation and exercise, with a trend towards identified regulation predicting initial/short-term adoption more strongly than intrinsic motivation, and intrinsic motivation being more predictive of long-term exercise adherence.
claim: More autonomous motivation goes with more exercise. Valuing the benefits (identified regulation) predicts starting; enjoying the activity itself (intrinsic motivation) predicts long-term adherence. Coach toward personally valued reasons early and toward enjoyment over time.
population: 66 studies of exercise and physical activity in adults, mostly non-experimental
used_for: framing motivation at intake and in long-term check-ins
caveat: Mostly correlational evidence.

quote: competence satisfaction and more intrinsic motives positively predict exercise participation across a range of samples and settings. Mixed evidence was found concerning the role of other types of motives (e.g., health/fitness and body-related)
claim: Feeling competent and having intrinsic motives consistently predict participation; health, fitness and body-related motives have mixed evidence. Do not rely on appearance as the main motivator.
population: exercise and physical activity studies in adults
used_for: goal framing; weight and appearance conversations
caveat: Mixed evidence for body-related motives; not proof that they are harmful.

quote: Increases in need support and autonomous motivation (but not controlled motivation or amotivation) were associated with positive changes in health behaviour. In conclusion, SDT-informed interventions positively affect indices of health; these effects are modest, heterogeneous
claim: Interventions based on self-determination theory improve health behaviour modestly; the improvement is linked to more support for autonomy, competence and relatedness and more autonomous motivation, not to pressure (controlled motivation).
population: 73 experimental studies across health behaviours (physical activity, diet, smoking and others)
used_for: autonomy-supportive coaching style
caveat: Effects are modest and heterogeneous.

quote: When using motivational interviewing in brief encounters of 15 minutes, 64% of the studies showed an effect. More than one encounter with the patient ensures the effectiveness of motivational interviewing.
claim: Motivational interviewing outperformed traditional advice-giving across many health behaviours; even brief 15-minute encounters showed an effect in 64% of studies, and more than one encounter improved effectiveness.
population: 72 RCTs across medical and psychological conditions, not specific to exercise
used_for: justifying short, repeated MI-style check-ins
caveat: Vote-count style figures; older review across diverse conditions.

quote: Interventions including motivational interviewing were superior to comparators for increases in total physical activity (SMD 0.45, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.65, equivalent to 1323 extra steps/day; low certainty evidence)
claim: Behavioural interventions that include motivational interviewing increased total physical activity by about 1300 steps per day versus comparators (SMD 0.45, low certainty evidence).
population: adults in 97 RCTs (median age 55.5, median BMI 28.9), mostly with a health condition
used_for: evidence for MI-style coaching conversations

quote: Evidence for a difference in any outcome compared with comparators of similar intensity was lacking. The magnitude of effect diminished over time, and evidence of an effect of motivational interviewing beyond one year was lacking.
claim: When MI was compared with other interventions of similar intensity, no added effect was shown, and the effect faded over time with no evidence beyond one year. The benefit may come from contact and structure as much as from MI itself; keep contact going and do not treat MI as sufficient alone.
population: adults in 97 RCTs; MVPA effect not shown in general-population samples
used_for: calibrating claims about MI; need for ongoing support
caveat: Certainty low to very low; most studies at high risk of bias.

quote: these are based upon expert opinion, and currently lack normative or other validity data to support them. ... % CR 40% 50% R:Q 1:1 2:1
claim: MI fidelity coding treats at least one reflection per question as fair and two reflections per question as good, with 40% (fair) to 50% (good) of reflections being complex (adding meaning rather than repeating). The manual states these thresholds are expert opinion without validity data. Use them as a style target: listen and reflect more than you question.
number: R:Q 1:1 fair, 2:1 good; complex reflections 40% fair, 50% good
population: clinicians delivering MI (developed in addiction treatment)
used_for: conversational style of intake and check-ins
caveat: Thresholds lack validity data; designed for coding recorded human sessions, not chat.

quote: To be considered an Affirm, the utterance must be about client's strengths, efforts, intentions, or worth. ... Affirm should not be coded automatically for the clinician's agreeing with, approval of, cheerleading for, or non-specific praising of the client. They must be explicitly linked to client behaviors or specific characteristics.
claim: An affirmation names a specific, genuine strength, effort or intention of the person; generic praise or cheerleading does not count. In check-ins, affirm concrete effort (for example getting two sessions done in a hard week) rather than saying 'great job'.
population: MI practice (expert definition)
used_for: tone of check-ins and feedback

quote: Persuade with Permission is assigned when the interviewer includes an emphasis on collaboration or autonomy support while persuading. ... 2. The clinician asks the client directly for permission to provide advice, make suggestions, give opinion, offer feedback, express concerns
claim: When giving advice or voicing a concern, first ask permission or frame it so the person can weigh it themselves; advice without this is coded as MI-inconsistent persuasion.
population: MI practice (expert definition)
used_for: giving advice, raising safety concerns, declining unsafe requests

quote: This code is used when the clinician confronts the client by directly and unambiguously disagreeing, arguing, correcting, shaming, blaming, criticizing, labeling, warning, moralizing, ridiculing, or questioning the client's honesty.
claim: Confrontation (arguing, shaming, blaming, labelling, moralising, questioning honesty) is MI-inconsistent. When a plan was missed or an unsafe request is made, avoid these; reflect, state facts neutrally and offer options.
population: MI practice (expert definition)
used_for: tone after missed sessions; refusing unsafe requests

quote: These are utterances that clearly focus the responsibility with the client for decisions about and actions pertaining to change. They highlight clients' sense of control, freedom of choice, personal autonomy, or ability or obligation to decide about their attitudes and actions.
claim: Emphasising autonomy means stating explicitly that decisions belong to the person (for example 'it is your call how many days you train this week').
population: MI practice (expert definition)
used_for: autonomy-supportive language in plans and refusals

quote: A random effects model indicated a small positive unique effect of goal setting across a range of behaviors, d = .34 (CI [.28, .41]). Moderator analyses indicated that goal setting was particularly effective if the goal was: (a) difficult, (b) set publicly, and (c) was a group goal.
claim: Goal setting on its own has a small positive effect on behaviour (d = 0.34); it worked better when goals were difficult, made public or set as group goals.
population: 141 papers, 384 effect sizes, N = 16,523, many behaviours
used_for: goal setting at intake
caveat: The 'difficult goal' moderator conflicts with advice to avoid hard specific goals for beginners (see Swann 2026).

quote: Overall, a medium, positive effect (Cohen's d(SE) = .552(.06), 95% CI = .43-.67, Z = 9.03, p < .001) of goal setting interventions in relation to PA behaviour was found.
claim: Multi-component goal-setting interventions (goals plus techniques such as feedback and self-monitoring) had a medium positive effect on physical activity (d = 0.55).
population: 45 articles, 52 interventions, n = 5912, diverse populations
used_for: goal setting combined with monitoring and feedback

quote: our review suggests that the SMART acronym: is not based on scientific theory; is not consistent with empirical evidence; does not consider what type of goal is set; is not applied consistently; is lacking detailed guidance; has redundancy in its criteria; is not being used as originally intended; and has a risk of potentially harmful effects.
claim: The SMART acronym is a widely used rule of thumb without a theoretical or empirical basis for physical activity goals, applied inconsistently, and may have harmful effects when goals are set badly. Do not treat SMART as the default goal format.
population: physical activity promotion (narrative review)
used_for: goal format choice
caveat: Narrative critique; SMART remains common practice and is required by some policies.

quote: a meta-analysis [3] found that specific goals were no more effective at increasing physical activity than vague goals such as to 'be more active', suggesting that, at least in some cases, goals do not need to be specific to be effective.
claim: Specific goals were no more effective than vague goals for increasing physical activity (citing McEwan 2016); goals do not have to be specific to work.
population: physical activity interventions
used_for: goal format choice

quote: specific challenging performance goals are likely to be most effective for increasing physical activity among individuals who are already active [13, 18]. ... while insufficiently active individuals walked further with open goals (e.g. 'see how many steps you can reach today') than with specific/SMART goals and reported more adaptive psychological outcomes
claim: Match goal type to activity level: for people already active, specific challenging performance goals work best; for insufficiently active people, open goals ('see how many steps you can reach today') produced more activity and better psychological responses than SMART goals.
population: adults; active vs insufficiently active (small walking studies)
used_for: goal setting for beginners vs trained athletes
caveat: Open-goal evidence comes from a few small studies by the authors' group.

quote: if individuals are new to exercise, or consider the process of increasing their physical activity to be complex, goal-setting theory suggests that specific challenging performance goals should not be used
claim: For people new to exercise or new to a complex skill (for example a new lift or climbing technique), avoid specific challenging performance goals; use learning goals (find and try strategies) or open goals instead.
population: novices and people learning complex tasks
used_for: beginner goal setting

quote: practitioners should minimise the likelihood of failing to achieve the goal, for example, by avoiding goals that are too difficult, providing goal striving/implementation strategies, or by using open goals.
claim: Minimise the chance of goal failure: avoid goals that are too difficult, add implementation strategies, or use open goals; failing an all-or-nothing goal can lower mood, self-esteem and motivation even when activity increased.
population: exercise clients
used_for: goal setting and goal review in check-ins

quote: Be able to combine multiple types of goal within programs to enable flexibility depending on circumstances and resources ... If the conditions aren't ideal for pursuing your primary goal, what other goals can you pursue instead?
claim: Combine several goal types in a programme and agree in advance on a fallback goal for when conditions are not ideal (for example a shorter minimum session when time or energy is low).
population: exercise clients
used_for: flexible planning, minimum viable session
caveat: Recommendation of an expert statement; the 'minimum session' application is an extrapolation.

quote: What has your experience of pursuing this goal been like? To what extent have you followed the desired behaviours? Would an additional/different goal help?
claim: In goal reviews, ask about the experience of pursuing the goal and adherence to the planned behaviours, not only about results, and adjust the goal if needed.
population: exercise clients
used_for: check-in question templates

quote: when goal difficulty is held constant, an assigned goal is as effective as one that is set participatively. The caveat is that the logic or rationale for the assigned goal must be given
claim: A goal suggested by the coach can work as well as one set together, provided the rationale is explained; setting it together may lead to higher goals and better understanding.
population: goal-setting theory (citing Latham)
used_for: explaining programme targets

quote: practitioners should consider and minimise the risk that goals could unintentionally exacerbate mental health symptoms, for example, by monitoring difficulty, supporting the client to disengage and re-set goals if necessary
claim: Watch for goals that create pressure, shame or anxiety; help the person step back and reset goals when needed.
population: exercise clients, especially those with mental health symptoms
used_for: goal review; referral awareness

quote: participants pursuing process goals had significantly greater adherence to an exercise programme compared to those pursuing outcome goals or a control group.
claim: Process goals (behaviours such as completing planned sessions) were linked to better programme adherence than outcome goals (citing Wilson and Brookfield).
population: exercise programme participants (single study cited)
used_for: goal type choice for adherence
caveat: Based on one cited study.

quote: Lally et al. [5] examined the formation of healthy eating, water consumption or exercise habits and reported that the median time to reach 95% automaticity was 66 days (range: 18 to 254 days).
claim: In the most cited habit study (citing Lally et al. 2010), new healthy eating, drinking or exercise habits took a median of 66 days to reach 95% automaticity, with a range of 18 to 254 days.
population: adult volunteers forming eating, drinking or exercise habits (Lally 2010, as reported by Singh 2024)
used_for: setting expectations about how long a new routine takes
caveat: Single study reported second-hand; the primary paper is paywalled and was not read.

quote: with the durations for individuals to form habits ranging from 4 to 335 days [5,22]. In summary, our results here, along with findings from others [5], clearly refute the popular notion that habits can be formed in approximately 21 days ... Individuals should anticipate a timeframe of at least two to five months to develop automaticity in new health habits
claim: Across studies, health habits took about two to five months to form, with individual times from 4 to 335 days; the popular 21-day figure is not supported.
population: 20 studies, 2601 participants, various health behaviours
used_for: expectation setting; avoiding 21-day challenge framing
caveat: Only 4 studies measured time to habit; most studies at high risk of bias.

quote: Frequency, timing, type of habit, individual choice, affective judgements, behavioural regulation and preparatory habits significantly influence habit strength, with morning practices and self-selected habits generally exhibiting greater strength.
claim: Habit strength was higher with frequent repetition, self-chosen behaviours, positive feelings about the behaviour and a consistent timing (morning practice was stronger in one stretching study).
population: 20 studies of health behaviours
used_for: habit design: let the person choose the behaviour and a stable cue
caveat: The morning advantage comes from a single study.

quote: It was found that exercising for at least four bouts per week for 6 weeks was the minimum requirement to establish an exercise habit.
claim: In new gym members, at least four exercise sessions per week for 6 weeks was the minimum associated with forming an exercise habit; consistency, low complexity, a supportive environment and enjoyment predicted habit growth.
number: 6 weeks (at least four sessions per week)
population: 111 new gym members over 12 weeks, self-reported habit
used_for: habit expectations for new exercisers
caveat: Single study; shorter than the Lally estimate; self-report.

quote: Trainers should keep exercises fun and simple for new clients and focus on consistency which could lead to habit formation in nearly 6 weeks.
claim: Keep early sessions simple and enjoyable and prioritise consistency over volume for new exercisers.
population: new gym members
used_for: beginner programme design for adherence

quote: PA was better promoted in the planned intervention group compared to the control group (SMD = 0.35, 95% CI = 0.25-0.44, I2 = 61.4%). Based on the subgroup analyses, we found that planning strategies were more effective among patients, males, when adopting AP intervention, when using the face-to-face sessions delivery mode, and when reinforcements were conducted during the follow-up.
claim: Planning interventions (action plans: when, where, how; coping plans: what to do if a barrier arises) increased physical activity (SMD 0.35); effects were larger when plans were reinforced during follow-up.
population: 41 RCTs, 5439 participants, general population
used_for: if-then plans at intake, revisited at check-ins

quote: The general survival curve shows that 63% of new members will abandon activities before the third month, and less than 4% will remain for more than 12 months of continuous activity.
claim: In an unsupervised gym setting, 63% of new members stopped within 3 months and fewer than 4% stayed continuously active for more than 12 months; the first 3 months are the highest-risk period.
number: 63% within 3 months; less than 4% beyond 12 months
population: 5240 members of one fitness centre in Brazil, 2005-2014
used_for: dropout risk awareness; early check-in frequency
caveat: One centre; membership cancellation is a proxy for stopping exercise.

quote: age, previous level of physical activity, initial body mass index and motivations related to weight loss, hypertrophy, health, and aesthetics are related to risk of abandonment.
claim: Age, prior activity level, starting BMI and the stated motive (weight loss, hypertrophy, health, aesthetics) were associated with risk of quitting; screen for these at intake.
population: fitness centre members in Brazil
used_for: intake risk assessment for dropout
caveat: Direction of each association not given in the abstract.

quote: The trim and fill adjusted pooled dropout rate across all interventions was 17.6% (95% confidence interval 14.2-21.5%).
claim: Supervised HIIT programmes for previously sedentary adults had a pooled dropout of about 18%.
population: 55 studies, 1318 sedentary healthy adults, programmes of 4 weeks or more
used_for: dropout expectations for structured programmes
caveat: Research settings with supervision; real-world dropout is higher (see Sperandei 2016).

quote: Longer session time (β = 0.02, P < 0.05), higher time effort/week (β = 0.005, P < 0.05), and overall time effort/intervention (β = 0.0003, P < 0.05) predicted greater dropout. Exercise intensity was not related to dropout.
claim: Longer sessions and more time per week predicted more dropout, while exercise intensity did not; for sedentary beginners, keep sessions short and the weekly time demand modest.
population: sedentary healthy adults in HIIT programmes
used_for: session length for beginners; minimum viable session

quote: Of the 29 trials that met all inclusion criteria, 21 (72%) achieved maintenance. ... intervention characteristics (longer duration [>24 weeks], face-to-face contact, use of more intervention strategies [>6], and use of follow-up prompts).
claim: Trials that maintained physical activity or diet change after the programme ended tended to last more than 24 weeks, include face-to-face contact, use more than 6 strategies and send follow-up prompts after the main phase.
number: 21 of 29 trials (72%); more than 24 weeks; more than 6 strategies
population: adults in 29 physical activity and dietary trials
used_for: programme length and post-programme prompts
caveat: Descriptive features of successful trials, not tested causes.

quote: The meta-analysis showed a small-to-moderate positive effect on physical activity measures (SDM 0.350, 95% CI 0.236 to 0.465, I2=69%, T 2=0.051) corresponding to 1850 steps per day (95% CI 1247 to 2457). Interventions including text-messaging and personalisation features were significantly more effective
claim: App and activity-tracker interventions increased physical activity by about 1850 steps per day (SDM 0.35); interventions with text messaging and personalisation were more effective.
population: 28 RCTs, 7454 adults aged 18-65 without chronic illness
used_for: value of tracking, messaging and personalisation
caveat: Long-term engagement and effect durability not established.

quote: Meta-analysis results showed significant effects (all p < 0.05) of chatbots for increasing total physical activity (SMD = 0.28 [95% CI = 0.16, 0.40]), daily steps (SMD = 0.28 [95% CI = 0.17, 0.39]), MVPA (SMD = 0.53 [95% CI = 0.24, 0.83])
claim: Chatbot interventions increased total physical activity (SMD 0.28), daily steps (SMD 0.28) and MVPA (SMD 0.53).
population: 19 trials, ages 9-71, mostly targeting physical activity
used_for: evidence base for an AI coach
caveat: 74% of trials low quality; most 6 weeks or shorter; mostly pre-LLM chatbots.

quote: Over half of the studies (n = 11, 58%) had a sample size of 75 or less and there was limited evidence examining longer-term impacts of chatbots, with most studies (n = 11, 58%) being 6 weeks or less, and no interventions being longer than 1 year.
claim: Chatbot evidence is short and small: 58% of studies had 75 or fewer participants and 58% lasted 6 weeks or less; there is no evidence beyond 1 year.
population: chatbot lifestyle trials
used_for: stating the limits of AI coaching honestly

quote: they cannot truly empathize and are limited in their understanding of a user's complete situation. Consequently, users may reveal sensitive information to an AI algorithm that lacks the capacity to handle such information suitably.
claim: AI chatbots cannot truly empathise and understand only part of a user's situation; users may disclose sensitive information the system cannot handle appropriately, so the coach must hand over to humans when that happens.
population: AI chatbots for lifestyle behaviour (authors' discussion)
used_for: escalation and referral when sensitive issues are disclosed

quote: Chatbots should have clear and transparent privacy policies, preferably leaving decisions around data retention in the hands of the user.
claim: Be transparent about data collection and retention and leave retention choices to the user.
population: AI chatbots (authors' recommendation)
used_for: privacy statements at intake

quote: The chatbot-based EIs significantly enhanced PA compared to control groups (SMD = 0.20, 95% CI = 0.04-0.37, p = 0.02; I² = 51%, p = 0.04). However, these interventions did not significantly impact EH (SMD = 0.29, 95% CI = -0.48-1.06, p = 0.46)
claim: In RCTs only, chatbot-based exercise interventions gave a small increase in physical activity (SMD 0.20) and no significant effect on exercise habits overall.
population: 12 RCTs, 2446 participants, ages 8-71
used_for: calibrating expectations of AI coaching

quote: AI-generated exercise recommendations were 41.2% (107/260) comprehensive and 90.7% (146/161) accurate, with the majority (8/15, 53%) of inaccuracy related to the need for exercise preparticipation medical clearance.
claim: An AI chatbot's exercise recommendations covered only 41% of expected content and were 91% accurate; most errors concerned preparticipation medical clearance. An AI coach must apply screening rules explicitly rather than rely on its general knowledge.
number: 41.2% comprehensive; 90.7% accurate; 53% of errors on clearance
population: AI chatbot prompted for 26 clinical populations
used_for: known limitations of AI exercise advice; screening

quote: Average readability level of AI-generated exercise recommendations was at the college level (mean 13.7, SD 1.7), with an average Flesch reading ease score of 31.1 (SD 7.7).
claim: AI-generated exercise advice was written at college reading level; use short, plain sentences.
population: AI chatbot output
used_for: readability of coach messages

quote: Adults and children who experience weight-based stigma are more likely to avoid exercise and physical activity, and to engage in unhealthy diets and sedentary behaviors that increase the risk of worsening obesity.
claim: Weight stigma makes people more likely to avoid exercise and physical activity; stigmatising communication undermines the coach's goal.
population: adults and children with overweight or obesity
used_for: weight and body conversations

quote: Both observational and randomized-controlled studies show that these strategies can result in the opposite effect, and may instead induce exercise avoidance, consumption of unhealthy diets, and increased sedentary behaviors
claim: Shame-based motivation backfires: it can cause exercise avoidance, unhealthy eating and more sedentary behaviour. Never use shame, fear about body size, or blame as a motivator.
population: people with overweight or obesity
used_for: tone of all check-ins; refusing crash-diet requests without blame

quote: To refrain from using stereotypical language, images, and narratives that unfairly and inaccurately depict individuals with overweight and obesity as lazy, gluttonous, and lacking willpower or self-discipline.
claim: Do not use language or narratives that portray people with higher body weight as lazy, gluttonous or lacking willpower.
population: people with overweight or obesity
used_for: coaching language rules

quote: body-weight regulation is not entirely under volitional control, and that biological, genetic, and environmental factors critically contribute to obesity.
claim: Body weight is not entirely under voluntary control; biology, genetics and environment contribute. Do not imply that weight outcomes reflect effort or character, and frame goals around behaviours the person controls.
population: people with overweight or obesity
used_for: framing weight-related goals as process goals

quote: neutral terminology (eg, "weight" or "unhealthy weight") is preferred and that words like "obese" and "fat" are least acceptable, particularly in provider-patient conversations about weight. However, individual variation in language preferences is evident
claim: People generally prefer neutral words such as 'weight'; 'obese' and 'fat' are least acceptable in professional conversations. Preferences vary, so ask which terms the person prefers.
population: 33 studies, 1999-2019, mostly Western samples
used_for: weight terminology in conversation

quote: whereas people do perceive greater uncertainty when it is communicated, we observed only a small decrease in trust in numbers and trustworthiness of the source, and mostly for verbal uncertainty communication.
claim: Stating uncertainty openly caused only a small drop in trust, mostly when the uncertainty was expressed in words rather than numbers; state uncertainty, preferably as a range.
population: five experiments, n = 5780 members of the public, non-health topics
used_for: explaining contested or uncertain evidence to athletes
caveat: Public news facts, not coaching conversations.

quote: First, in the preparation stage, practitioners should seek to understand the client's background and circumstances ... Third, the planning stage is concerned with preparing for goal striving and includes the development of goal commitment, identification of barriers and strategies to attainment, and the establishment of strategies for feedback and monitoring. Finally, once goal implementation/striving has begun, the follow-up stage can involve reinforcement of goal progress, goal revision
claim: Run goal setting in four stages: preparation (understand background, circumstances and why the goal matters), goal setting, planning (commitment, barriers, strategies, feedback and monitoring) and follow-up (reinforce progress, revise goals).
population: exercise clients (synthesised model cited by ESSA, Bird et al.)
used_for: structure of the intake conversation and later goal reviews

quote: Fifty-five articles were finally included. Fourteen key factors were identified as relevant to increase adherence to physical exercise by at least ten reviews: (a) characteristics of the exercise program, (b) involvement of professionals from different disciplines, (c) supervision, (d) technology,
claim: An umbrella review of 55 articles named 14 factors that at least ten reviews linked to better exercise adherence in chronic disease and older adults; the first four are the exercise programme itself, multidisciplinary professionals, supervision and technology.
population: adults with chronic diseases and older adults
used_for: adherence factors: programme, supervision, technology
caveat: Factors are counted by how often reviews mention them; the review gives no effect sizes.

quote: (e) initial exploration of participant's characteristics, barriers, and facilitators, (f) participants education, adequate expectations and knowledge about risks and benefits, (g) enjoyment and absence of unpleasant experiences, (h) integration in daily living, (i) social support and relatedness, (j) communication and feedback,
claim: Adherence factors for chronic disease and older adults include an initial exploration of the person's barriers and facilitators, education and realistic expectations, enjoyment, integration in daily living, social support and relatedness, and communication and feedback.
population: adults with chronic diseases and older adults
used_for: intake questions and check-in content for older or chronic clients
caveat: Counted by frequency in reviews, not effect size.

quote: (k) available progress information and monitoring, (l) self-efficacy and competence, (m) participant's active role and (n) goal setting.
claim: Further adherence factors are progress information and monitoring, self-efficacy and competence, an active role for the participant and goal setting.
population: adults with chronic diseases and older adults
used_for: adherence: monitoring, competence, active role
caveat: Counted by frequency in reviews, not effect size.

quote: Although results varied, no consistent differences in attrition or adherence rates between sustained and intermittent exercise protocols were revealed.
claim: In 14 RCTs of aerobic exercise (mean age 42), results varied and there was no consistent difference in attrition or adherence between sustained and intermittent (split) exercise protocols.
population: adults, mean age 42, 76% female, mostly healthy
used_for: session format (long vs split sessions) and adherence
caveat: Abstract only; RCTs of 8 weeks to 18 months in volunteers. It contrasts with BEH-42, where longer sessions and more weekly time predicted dropout in sedentary HIIT trials.

quote: the result found in the subgroup with reinforcement of the implementation intentions strategy was 0.25 (IC 95% = 0.05-0.45) in favor of the intervention group.
claim: Implementation intentions (if-then plans) that were reinforced during follow-up increased physical activity in adults, with a pooled effect of 0.25 (95% CI 0.05-0.45); 13 RCTs.
population: adults aged 18-76 with mixed conditions (coronary disease, obesity, diabetes, sedentary)
used_for: if-then plans, reinforce at check-ins
caveat: Small effect with a wide interval; the subgroup without reinforcement is not reported in the abstract.

quote: equating to approximately 1800 extra steps per day, 40 min per day more walking, and reductions of approximately 1 kg in bodyweight.
claim: In an umbrella review, activity trackers added about 1800 steps per day, 40 min per day of walking and about 1 kg lower body weight, with small and often non-significant effects on blood pressure, cholesterol and other physiological outcomes.
population: clinical and non-clinical populations of all ages (39 reviews)
used_for: tracker: expected effect size
caveat: Review-level pooled estimates; heterogeneity between reviews was not quantified in the abstract.

quote: Activity trackers appear to be effective at increasing physical activity in a variety of age groups and clinical and non-clinical populations. The benefit is clinically important and is sustained over time.
claim: The authors judge activity trackers effective for increasing physical activity across age groups and populations, with a clinically important benefit that is sustained over time, and recommend their use.
population: all age groups, clinical and non-clinical populations
used_for: tracker as default tool
caveat: Abstract only; how long sustained is not stated in the abstract.

quote: The sample-weighted average effect size for SDT interventions was d+ = .23, and there were significant effects for physical activity, sedentary behavior, diet, alcohol consumption, and smoking cessation (.16 ≥ d+ ≥ .29).
claim: Self-determination-theory interventions had a small average effect on health behaviour (d+ = 0.23; range 0.16 to 0.29 across physical activity, sedentary behaviour, diet, alcohol and smoking); autonomous motivation and perceived competence mediated the effect.
population: adults and young people in 65 SDT intervention tests across health behaviours
used_for: autonomy support: expected effect size
caveat: Publication bias and small-study bias were present; after correction the effect stayed above zero but smaller (d+ of at least 0.15).

quote: This review highlights the promising applications of LLMs in ERs and PA but emphasizes that they remain a supplement to human expertise. Expert validation is essential to ensure safety and mitigate risks.
claim: A scoping review of large-language-model exercise recommendations concludes they are a supplement to human expertise and that expert validation is essential for safety.
population: clinical and healthy populations; studies up to March 2024
used_for: AI coach supervised by a human
caveat: Scoping review of 11 mostly low-powered studies; not a test of effectiveness.

quote: 1.8% (11/598) of studies were included after screening and applying selection criteria. ... 45% (5/11) of the studies used experimental designs to evaluate LLM interventions in ERs and PA.
claim: Only 11 of 598 screened papers on large language models for exercise recommendations qualified, and only 5 of the 11 used experimental designs, so controlled evidence is very thin.
population: clinical and healthy populations; studies up to March 2024
used_for: LLM coaching: evidence is thin
caveat: Search ended March 2024, so newer work is not included.

quote: Contrary to the popular belief in a "magic number" of days to develop a habit, we find that it typically takes months to form the habit of going to the gym but weeks to develop the habit of handwashing in the hospital.
claim: In over 12 million gym-attendance observations, forming a gym habit typically took months, not a fixed number of days; handwashing took weeks.
population: gym members (objective attendance data) and hospital staff
used_for: habit timeline: months for gym
caveat: Observational, model-based estimate of habit formation; supports BEH-34.

quote: Five overarching, interconnected themes representing theoretical explanations for behaviour change maintenance emerged. Theoretical explanations of behaviour change maintenance focus on the differential nature and role of motives, self-regulation, resources (psychological and physical), habits, and environmental and social influences from initiation to maintenance.
claim: A review of 100 behaviour theories found five themes for maintaining behaviour change: motives, self-regulation, psychological and physical resources, habits, and environmental and social influences.
population: behaviour-change theories, general population
used_for: what to review in maintenance check-ins
caveat: Theory synthesis, not trial evidence; it is a checklist for check-ins, not proof of effect.

quote: Discuss with the person any concerns or barriers that may affect their attendance and participation in the intervention (such as personal circumstances, cultural barriers, physical health needs, or neurodevelopmental or psychological factors)
claim: NICE: providers should discuss with each person the concerns or barriers that may affect attendance (personal circumstances, cultural barriers, physical health needs, neurodevelopmental or psychological factors), repeat the discussion during the programme if needed, and acknowledge progress and experiences.
population: adults in behavioural weight-management services (UK guideline)
used_for: check-in: ask about barriers repeatedly
caveat: Written for weight-management service providers, not for athletes.

quote: discuss whether the programme is suitable for them at this time if it has not been possible to resolve their difficulties with the intervention agree what should happen next (for example, referral to another service, leave the intervention at an agreed time, or think about a re-referral at a later date)
claim: NICE: when someone has difficulties that stop them taking part, discuss whether the programme suits them at this time and, if it cannot be resolved, agree the next step (referral, leaving at an agreed time, or re-referral later).
population: adults in behavioural weight-management services (UK guideline)
used_for: stepping back or pausing a plan without blame
caveat: Written for weight-management service providers.

quote: Promptly follow up those who miss sessions to establish why, ensure safeguarding, and encourage re-engagement.
claim: NICE (children and young people's services): follow up promptly with those who miss sessions to find out why, ensure safeguarding, and encourage them to re-engage.
population: children and young people in behavioural weight-management services (UK guideline)
used_for: missed-session follow-up
caveat: The recommendation is for young people's services, used here as the closest guideline wording; no trial tests the follow-up timing.
